content: Dr. Alison Edelman serves as a consultant on the European Advisory Board of Exelgyn. She is also a co-investigator in research studies funded by the United States National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the Society of Family Planning (USA). The research unit she collaborates with receives ongoing funding from MSD and Bayer Healthcare to conduct studies on the acceptability, efficacy, and safety of contraceptive pills, transdermal patches, and hormone-releasing intrauterine devices. Dr. Anna Glasier acts as an expert consultant for HRA Pharma (France). Her husband occasionally consults for HRA Pharma, approximately once every two years, as a member of a scientific advisory board and less frequently participates as a speaker or chairperson at international conferences on behalf of the company. Dr. Glasier specifically works with HRA Pharma on developing new methods of emergency contraception (EC). She was the principal investigator of a large randomized controlled trial that led to the marketing of ulipristal acetate (UPA) for EC. While she did not receive personal remuneration, the clinic where she conducted the research received funding. Since the publication of the study results in 2010, Dr. Glasier has been actively involved and receives a regular consultancy fee to advise HRA Pharma on obtaining approval for over-the-counter use of UPA and on research related to EC effectiveness based on user body weight. She is also paid as a member of the company’s Scientific Advisory Board and participates as a speaker or chairperson at international conferences on behalf of the company, approximately twice a year. Dr. Glasier has provided expert opinions on UPA to regulatory authorities and represented HRA Pharma at these meetings. Due to her relationship with a company manufacturing EC, including UPA, she did not chair or participate in discussions on EC and weight at the March 2014 meeting and left the room when the inclusion of UPA in the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) and Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR) guidelines was discussed. Additionally, Dr. Glasier has an independent research grant from Pfizer Ltd (UK) to study the feasibility of pharmacists dispensing and administering a subcutaneously injected contraceptive. She also has an independent research grant from HRA Pharma to fund a clinical research fellow for up to three years to conduct research in contraception. Dr. Andy Gray works at CAPRISA, a research unit that receives donations of antiretroviral medications from the NIH Clinical Research Products Management Center. These donations include products manufactured by Abbott, Boehringer Ingelheim, Bristol Myers Squibb, Gilead, GlaxoSmithKline, MSD, and Roche for use in clinical trials conducted through the AIDS Clinical Trials Group and the International Maternal, Paediatric, Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trial Network. The unit also received donated microbicide products from Gilead Sciences for a Phase IIb clinical trial. Dr. Philip Hannaford works in an academic department that previously received fees from several manufacturers of oral contraceptives for lectures on contraception, particularly oral contraception, during scientific meetings supported by these pharmaceutical companies. Dr. Olav Meirik received $5,000 from the WHO in 2013 to conduct a survey estimating the patterns of combined oral contraceptive use among formulations containing 3rd and 4th generation progestogens. He also serves as an unpaid senior research associate with the Instituto Chileno de Medicina Reproductiva (ICMER). Dr. Chelsea Polis collaborated on a trial investigating the acceptability of a subcutaneous injectable contraceptive. Data collection for this study ceased in 2013. Pfizer, Inc. donated the injectable units, which were not yet commercially available, to her research unit for the trial but did not provide monetary support. Dr. Régine Sitruk-Ware received €1,500 twice over a four-year period from Bayer to provide lectures on future targets for non-hormonal contraceptives in the female reproductive tract. She also received €4,500 in 2014 from MSD to advise on the development of a progestin, nomegestrol acetate. Due to her research on the development of the progesterone-releasing vaginal ring, Dr. Sitruk-Ware did not participate in deliberations that led to the inclusion of this method in the guidelines or the formulation of recommendations for its use. Dr. Lisa Soule is employed by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), a regulatory body for hormonal contraceptives in the USA. At the meeting, she represented the interests of the FDA, which serves public health rather than commercial interests. Dr. Carolyn Westhoff receives an honorarium from Agile Therapeutics to serve on its Scientific Advisory Board, approximately $2,500 per quarter. She also receives honoraria as a member of the Data Safety and Monitoring Boards of both MSD and Bayer Healthcare to monitor contraceptive safety studies conducted by these companies, approximately $3,500 per year and €2,700 per year, respectively. Her research unit receives funding to conduct studies on intrauterine devices (Bayer Healthcare and Medicine 360), a trial on the efficacy of self-administration of an injectable contraceptive method (Pfizer, Inc.), and a trial on the safety and effectiveness of oral contraceptive pills (MSD). Dr. Julie Williams is employed by the United Kingdom’s Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). She served as the lead rapporteur for the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Article 31 referral for combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), which assessed the risk of venous thromboembolism across different products and how this influenced the balance of benefits and risks. The review was considered by the EMA’s Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC), and the resulting PRAC recommendation and Committee on Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) Opinion were made publicly available on the EMA website. These reviews led to changes in the product information for CHCs included in the Article 31 referral. The systematic reviews conducted as part of the development of the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (Fifth Edition) included reviews of epidemiological, clinical, and pharmacological evidence. These reviews, some of which were published in peer-reviewed journals, are available through open access and will be periodically updated as new reviews are published.
